subject.title: New Stanzas for Amazing Grace
subject.author: Allen Ginsberg
subject.text:
I dreamed I dwelled in a homeless place
Where I was lost alone
Folk looked right through me into space
And passed with eyes of stone

O homeless hand on many a street
Accept this change from me
A friendly smile or word is sweet
As fearless charity

Woe workingman who hears the cry
And cannot spare a dime
Nor look into a homeless eye
Afraid to give the time

So rich or poor no gold to talk
A smile on your face
The homeless ones where you may walk
Receive amazing grace

I dreamed I dwelled in a homeless place
Where I was lost alone
Folk looked right through me into space
And passed with eyes of stone
  April 2, 1994

Composed at the request of Ed Sanders for his production of The New Amazing
Grace, performed November 20, 1994, at the Poetry Project in St. Mark ' s Church
in-the-Bouwerie

title: The Slave Trader's Hymn, Reissued for 1994
standfirst: In April 1994, three months into a mayoralty that had just begun arresting New Yorkers for looking too visibly poor, Allen Ginsberg took a commission from an old comrade and wrote four new stanzas into a two-hundred-year-old redemption hymn by a former slave-ship captain. It looks like a detour from Howl. It wasn't — he'd rehearsed this exact move for twenty-five years.

sections.heading: Handed a Melody, He Filled In the Words
sections.body:
The date under the poem's last line is precise: April 2, 1994. Ginsberg wrote it as an assignment, not a summons from within — a printed note under the text explains that Ed Sanders had asked him for a contribution to *The New Amazing Grace*, a project built on one blunt idea: take the old hymn's tune and stanza shape and hand out blank verses for whoever would fill them in. Sanders had standing to ask. He and Ginsberg went back to the earliest days of the Lower East Side scene that made both their reputations — Sanders had run the Peace Eye Bookstore at 383 East Tenth Street since the early 1960s, a gathering point that [became known for Bohemians, writers and radicals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Sanders), and co-founded the rock band the Fugs in 1964. He later wrote a book-length poem about Ginsberg's own life and work. This was a favor between neighbors of thirty years' standing.

The poem's printed note dates its premiere to November 20, 1994, at the Poetry Project inside St. Mark's Church in-the-Bowery, a few blocks from where Sanders had kept his bookstore. The production kept running: a surviving performer's script for a second edition, [*New Amazing Grace II*](https://www.granarybooks.com/pages/books/2033/edward-sanders/new-amazing-grace-ii?soldItem=true), documents a further Poetry Project benefit a year later, on November 15, 1995, with Ginsberg again on the bill alongside Robert Creeley, Pete Seeger, Anne Waldman and Jim Carroll. Whatever else it was, it was an ongoing production, and Ginsberg kept showing up to it.

sections.heading: The Words Belonged to a Reformed Slave-Ship Captain
sections.body:
The hymn Sanders was recycling did not start out as consolation. Newton wrote it, under the title *Faith's Review and Expectation*, for a New Year's prayer meeting on 1 January 1773, in the Buckinghamshire market town of Olney, where he had been curate since 1764. He was already at sea when a violent storm off the Irish coast, on 10 March 1748, prompted what he later called his conversion. It didn't end his career: over the following six years, now as captain, he ran three more voyages carrying enslaved Africans to the West Indies — work he later admitted he saw at the time as ["an easy and creditable way of life"](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Newton) — and only left the sea in 1754, when poor health forced the decision. The hymn was published five years after that Olney meeting, in the 1779 collection *Olney Hymns*, compiled with the poet William Cowper. Its theme of grace given to someone who did nothing to earn it carries that biography, whether or not any single verse names it.

The tune everyone now hears under Newton's words wasn't there at first. ["New Britain"](https://www.hymnologyarchive.com/amazing-grace) wasn't paired with the text until 1835, when William Walker printed it in his shape-note tunebook *Southern Harmony* — fifty-six years after the words themselves appeared. That gap is possible because both words and tune sit inside common meter: four lines, alternating eight and six syllables, rhyming *abab*, [the same skeleton behind hundreds of English hymns and ballads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_metre), interchangeable by design. Ginsberg's four stanzas keep Newton's count to the syllable; the tune under his words never had to change.

sections.heading: He Had Been Rehearsing This for Twenty-Five Years
sections.body: None of this required Ginsberg to reach outside his usual register, whatever it looked like from outside. In 1948, in a Harlem apartment, he had what he described for the rest of his life as a vision of William Blake reciting poetry to him. Two decades later, in 1969, he [set the whole of Blake's *Songs of Innocence and of Experience* to music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songs_of_Innocence_and_Experience_%28Allen_Ginsberg_album%29), recording it over two months at Apostolic Studios in New York with a harmonium under his own hands; the record came out the following year. He had carried that harmonium into readings ever since, sometimes to accompany chanted Hare Krishna mantras rather than his own lines. In 1974 he helped Chögyam Trungpa and Anne Waldman found the Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics at the Naropa Institute in Boulder, formalizing a Buddhist practice he had by 1994 kept up for two decades, alongside a standing post, since 1986, as Distinguished Professor of English at Brooklyn College. A poet with that record didn't need to improvise a hymn voice for Sanders in April 1994. He had one on file.

sections.heading: The City Outside the Church Door
sections.body:
Ginsberg dated his poem three months into a new mayoralty. Rudy Giuliani took office on January 1, 1994; his first police commissioner, William Bratton, spent that year building an enforcement strategy around the broken-windows theory, aimed squarely at behavior associated with visible poverty. One of its first targets was the city's squeegee men, panhandlers who washed windshields at stopped traffic and demanded payment; a study by the criminologist George Kelling found that [three-quarters of them weren't actually homeless and that half had felony records](https://www.city-journal.org/article/the-professional-panhandling-plague), and police used that finding to justify arresting them for blocking traffic. The city opened a Midtown Community Court that year built specifically to fast-track quality-of-life arrests — someone cited for panhandling in the morning could be sentenced to community service and back on the street cleaning it that afternoon. Enforcement of statutes against panhandling and loitering, long left largely unused, expanded from Midtown outward.

Read against that timeline, the poem's refrain sounds less like a general complaint about urban indifference than a description of a newly organized civic posture: "Folk looked right through me into space / And passed with eyes of stone." St. Mark's Church, where the piece premiered eight months later, sits a few blocks from Tompkins Square Park, which [the city had shut for renovation from June 1991 to July 1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tompkins_Square_Park) specifically to clear the homeless encampment that had made the park a flashpoint since a police riot there over an earlier curfew in August 1988. Nobody in that room in November 1994 needed the recent history explained to them.

sections.heading: A Coin Called Change, Three Years Before the End
sections.body:
Newton's hymn speaks in one voice, addressed to nobody but God and the singer's own conscience. Ginsberg's four new stanzas split that address in two. The first speaks to "homeless hand on many a street," offering "this change from me" — one word doing two jobs, coins pressed into a palm and the personal shift the poem is asking for, collapsed into a single syllable. The second turns to someone else entirely: "Woe workingman who hears the cry / And cannot spare a dime." Newton's hymn has one speaker examining his own soul. Ginsberg's has a speaker addressing two different classes of stranger, inside the same eight bars.

> I dreamed I dwelled in a homeless place
> Where I was lost alone
> Folk looked right through me into space
> And passed with eyes of stone

That quatrain opens the poem and, unchanged, closes it — a dream that returns the reader exactly to where it started, a device with no equivalent anywhere in Newton's original four verses. And "fearless charity," the phrase Ginsberg uses for the "friendly smile or word" that costs nothing, reaches toward something Buddhist teaching names outright: [abhaya-dana, the gift of fearlessness](https://www.wisdomlib.org/definition/abhayadana), one of three traditional forms of dana alongside gifts of material goods and gifts of teaching. Ginsberg had been a practicing Buddhist for two decades by 1994; whether or not he meant the borrowing precisely, the vocabulary was close at hand.

He had three years left. The poem stayed uncollected until *Death & Fame: Last Poems 1993-1997* appeared in 1999, two years after Ginsberg died of liver cancer on April 5, 1997 — one of roughly seventy poems gathered from his final four years, built on a stanza shape he had kept in reserve since 1969, brought out once more for a stranger's spare change.
